extracted.intended_audience: students, playwrights, humor theorists, critics, and writers studying comedic theory and comedic technique
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical analysis of what produces the comic: archetypal mechanisms, devices, and dramatic arrangements that provoke laughter, illustrated with theatrical and literary examples. Useful for analyzing or designing comic situations and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic often arises when a person is perceived as an object or thing rather than as a fully living being — an impression of inanimate, mechanical or object-like qualities in a human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sancho Panza flung like a football; Baron Munchausen as a cannon-ball; clowns whose movements reduce them to balls or dummies. Use progressive blurring of human outline into a 'thing' to generate laughable images. Note: this is a central law/formula for many comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion: from vague to clear (method of suggestion par excellence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic impression can be built by starting from definite perceptions and making them progressively indefinite, or vice versa, so that imagination is led step-by-step to accept the ludicrous vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: employ a slow, graduated series of hints to convert a vague impression into a concrete comic image (like hypnotic suggestion). Poetic devices (rhythm, rhyme, assonance) can lull the imagination and prepare it to accept a suggested image (examples: lines of Regnard; Figaro passage). Useful for subtle or poetic comic suggestions rather than coarse physical jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion of person with function (feigned identity with role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating or speaking of a person as if they were merely a function or role — confusing the individual with the office or operation they perform — creates comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the mayor's line about the prefect 'who has been changed several times since 1847...' (function continues regardless of individual). Use to liken people to impersonal events or to suggest that the function operates independently of the person. Works especially when the audience already accepts circumstances that make the confusion plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANY ARRANGEMENT ... IS COMIC WHICH GIVES US THE ILLUSION OF LIFE AND THE DISTINCT IMPRESSION OF A MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Core definition: a combination of acts/events is comic when it simultaneously gives an impression of life and of mechanical arrangement (something living shown as mechanical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the broad archetype that underlies many comic devices. To create comedy, stage situations so life’s continuity is interrupted by visible mechanisms (strings, springs, gears), or make characters appear automated. Contrast living continuity (evolution, irreversibility, individuality) with mechanical traits (repetition, reversibility, interference) to provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jack-in-the-box (repetition as spring vs repression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition on stage (words, actions) symbolizes a repressed feeling that keeps springing out and an idea or force that delights in repressing it again; the recurring motion creates a mechanical impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Punch and Judy policeman repeatedly felled; Dorine/Orgon ('Et Tartuffe?') where the question recurs like a spring; Scapin playing with Geronte's avarice. Use repeated beats/phrases to suggest mechanical automatism — but ensure repetition feels tied to a moral/emotional struggle (repressed feeling vs repressive idea) rather than being meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of situations (dramatic recurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating an entire scene or combination of circumstances within a play (across acts or with different characters) creates comic coincidence and contrast with life's expected change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Molière's École des femmes and George Dandin reproduce the same incident in multiple 'tempi'; device of masters then servants repeating the same scene. Make repetitions naturally introduced and sufficiently complex to heighten the absurdity — the more complex and plausibly integrated, the funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack (manipulation / loss of agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: One character appears to be freely acting while actually being controlled by another (like a marionette), producing the impression of a living being guided by external strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scapin manipulating Geronte and Argante; characters vacillating between two contrary opinions personified as opposing agents. To use: personify opposing choices/voices and show a visible puppet-master influence; spectator often sides with the knave who pulls the strings. Emphasize apparent motion of control to create comic detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball (arithmetical progression / chain-reaction escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trivial initial cause grows by accumulation into a major, often absurdly disproportionate effect — the rolling-snowball/chain-reaction arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ninepins, toy soldiers/toppling, house of cards, Don Quixote inn scene, Labiche's hat that keeps slipping away, La Cagnotte circular return. Useful to construct sequences where each incident triggers a worse one; reversibility and circular return (ending where you began) intensify the comic effect. Ensure causal links are visible so mechanism is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility / circular return as intensifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical combinations are especially laughable when they are reversible or circular — when efforts and travels bring characters back to the starting point, making the great exertion result in nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Labiche comedies where characters end up where they began; Les Surprises du divorce returning husband to original wife. Use circular plotting to highlight futility; note caution: lack of proportion alone (great effect from small cause or vice versa) is not always comic unless it reveals mechanical arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three abstract comic processes: repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference of series
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy's essential methods correspond to the mechanical counterparts of life: (1) repetition of scenes/words, (2) inversion (reversal) of expected order/roles, and (3) reciprocal interference of series (parallel lines of events colliding and affecting each other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three processes are seen across examples given: repetition (see above); inversion (e.g., masters imitating servants or role reversals); reciprocal interference (interlocking series of causes and effects that upset one another). Use these archetypes as a checklist when designing comic situations; combine them for richer effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (role/order reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inverting the normal order or role relations (masters behaving like servants, anticipated outcome reversed) produces comic friction by violating the expected individuality and order of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Benedix's Der Eigensinn where masters reproduce a scene first set by servants in inverted order. To apply: swap social roles, reverse cause-effect order, or mirror a sequence with elements swapped to expose mechanical symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series (interlocking causal chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more sequences of events interfere with one another so that each alters or accelerates the other, producing escalating or absurd outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Plaideurs' lawsuits within lawsuits; Chicanneau's crowded law-terms; picture-book chain of accidents (tea spilt → elderman → window falls → constable struck → police commotion). Design parallel strands that collide to compound the comic effect; ensure audience can perceive the mechanical connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification of opposing decisions / inner duality device
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicting a single character as containing two opposed, inelastic impulses (e.g., frankness vs politeness) that alternate mechanically creates comic repetition and tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alceste ('I don't say that!') where the comic stems from the duel in one man between his misanthropic resolve and ingrained politeness. Use when you want verbal or behavioral oscillation to feel automatic and childish rather than fully human complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as detection of 'absentmindedness' in life; laughter as social corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic exposes a lapse or rigidity in the living continuity of life — a mechanical absentmindedness — and laughter functions as a social gesture that singles out and represses that imperfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive principle more than a how-to: design scenes where inelasticity, automatism, or absent-minded mechanical behavior in people or events is highlighted. The audience’s laughter acts to mark and correct the exposed social failing; thus comedic effects often carry implicit moral/social corrective force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and acceptability: a joke must be made acceptable by state of mind and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A witticism's success depends not only on its internal construction but on its fittingness to the character's state of mind and to the surrounding circumstances — acceptance occurs when it seems natural to the situation or to the speaker's psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: M. Perrichon's enumeration of parcels (Four, five... and myself nine) or the girl's phrase 'that have occurred' — the joke feels acceptable because it matches the character's excitement or repetitive lesson. When crafting comic lines, ensure they arise plausibly from character and context rather than feeling forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: lack of proportion is not by itself comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Disproportion between cause and effect (either great cause → small effect or small cause → great effect) is not automatically funny; its comic power comes only when it reveals an underlying mechanical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely solely on disproportion for humor. Instead, arrange the causal chain so the audience perceives the mechanicality or automatism that the disproportion uncovers. Test whether the mechanical arrangement is visible — if not, the disproportion may not provoke laughter.
